content.title: Response to Reviewer 9E3Y
content.comment:
Thank you for the comments and suggestions. We have added an Ethics Statement to the paper. Below we address your specific questions:

**Could you justify that the new taxonomy of generic reasoning errors can cover all the possible reasoning errors?** Thank you for this question. Indeed, our study is the first initial step that investigates the evaluation of the step-by-step reasoning produced by large language models. Our taxonomy (in Table 2) covers several reasoning errors and we designed our metrics to evaluate a spectrum of criteria including the ones in the taxonomy. Even though we cannot say we cover all possible reasoning errors, our metrics are generic enough, work on natural language rationales, and consider the alignment with the input context and the generated explanation. Nevertheless, we believe our study can spur others to investigate different reasoning errors and use our code and datasets as templates to extend further. We discuss this in the Limitations section in the paper (Appendix A) which we added to the revised version of the paper.
To see if our ROSCOE metrics can evaluate different types of reasoning errors based on our taxonomy of errors (in Table 2), we introduced synthetic perturbations (including negation). Please see Table 14: Synthetic perturbations and corresponding error types of steps. We tried to capture several reasoning errors including negation as a type of “factuality” and “coherency” error. We designed experiments on 6 datasets with synthetic perturbations as shown in Tables 20-25 with details of each perturbation (including negation). Our results indicate that ROSCOE metrics can more accurately capture such errors in comparison to all the strong baselines. 

**The authors argue that "The existing works primarily focus on end-task performance." However, it is unclear if the good performance of reasoning rationales (by the proposed ROSCOE) means a good performance on end-task performance.** Thank you for this feedback. We agree that, for generative tasks, it is possible for models to generate both strong rationales with the wrong answer or weak rationales with the right answer. It is still somewhat unproven in the literature whether correct rationales necessarily improve end-task performance (though there is strong evidence suggesting the presence of rationales does). As we do not explicitly extract exact match answers using templates (as done in say, the Chain of Thought line of work), we do not include correlations of our scores against this form of end task performance. However, our human annotations do include an Overall Quality evaluation, using the question “Does the generated response answer the question in a well-justified manner? (1=incomprehensible and wrong, 5=clear and correct)” which, in the annotation scheme we provided to our expert annotators in offline review, does ask as a proxy for end-task performance. We see in Tables 33-39 that the correlation of ROSCOE on this annotation question consistently exceeds those of baseline.   

**Many presentation logics should be improved. For example section 3, "To evaluate ROSCOE,", however, it is unclear what exactly “ROSCOE” is. And "ROSCOE" is itself a metric, how could we evaluate a metric?** Thank you for this feedback. As we mention in the abstract and the introduction, we use the term ROSCOE to refer to the *suite* of metrics we are proposing to evaluate the step-by-step reasoning and rationale generated by language models. So ROSCOE does not yield a scalar score (unlike our baseline scorers such as BARTScore [1] or CTC [3]). Instead, ROSCOE introduces several metrics which do yield multiple scalar values. Each individual metric measures fine-grained characteristics of language model reasoning and explanations from different perspectives (such as logical consistency or semantic coherence), providing a more interpretable and effective method of evaluation. Following the literature on evaluation of a new metric research [1,2,4], we meta-evaluate our ROSCOE metrics against baseline metrics by comparing each metric’s correlation with the synthetic perturbations and human-provided manual scores. Specifically, if a metric is highly correlated with the human judgements it is considered more effective based on the criteria the metric evaluates.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors collect data about rationale used in reasoning tasks. It includes two major datasets: "diagnostics" which includes human generated gold-reference rationale, and "judgements" which include machine generated rationale with human judged errors (see table 7 in the appendix for dataset statistics). Their suite of metrics is based off this data, and designed to measure the effectiveness of newly generated rationale. The metrics mostly are intrinsic, and don't account for downstream task performance that I can tell.

Regarding the rationale and metrics, I could be missing a crucial detail... It is mentioned in sec3 that the final step in the chain is the answer, but for the most part, I have interpreted this work as if the chain does not include the answer. Since some of the metrics would not make sense if the last step is the final answer.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths

* Substantial datasets including human-generated rationale. Also includes machine-generated rationale annotated with errors by humans.

* The dataset will enable new work to leverage the data directly to improve performance or create more rationale. But this is not all. We can use this data to measure the qualities of what is considered human-like rationale, and that is what this paper does by presenting a suite of metrics along with their analysis.

# Weaknesses

* Not nearly enough analysis and exploration of the new data. For example, do these rationale lead to improved (or worse) performance? Or categorizing different types of rationale and their properties.

* It should be made more clear what are the assumptions about rationale, e.g. do we expect there to be only one valid reasoning chain?

* There are clear downsides to the introduced metrics. The major one being I am not convinced they would recognize an equally good but different looking rationale. I don't think this is something the baseline metrics would be capable of doing, but also not convinced ROSCOE could do either. Perhaps challenging qualitative results would help. Although evaluating different types of rationale on a downstream task would be most informative.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is fairly clear and would be valuable to the community because it provides a valuable resources (the rationale related data) and example on how to use these for research (the metrics).

That being said, the data could be more closely analyzed and I am not convinced of the usefulness of the metrics.

I have many issues with the metrics, and describe a few below:

Faithfulness-Step: This seems very dependent on how you define steps. A chain-of-thought (CoT) can be only a few steps using multiple tokens each, and lead to deceptively high (or low) faithfulness scores. Is this the reason for the -token version?

Informativeness-Step: This seems counter intuitive to how CoT often works... CoT works especially well with natural language explanations, which probably will include text not in the source.

Repetition-token: Some prompt formats (e.g. least-to-most prompting) rely on repeating information from previous steps in order to gradually construct the answer, so will do poorly here...

Missing step: if there is a "budget" on how much can be done in the CoT, then it is potentially desirable to skip some steps and only elaborate on the most crucial ones. Also, one advantage of CoT is there are many possible reasoning chains (see self-consistency work for example).

Also in sec 4.4, the metrics based on perplexity seem somewhat strange --- isn't perplexity used to measure the model not the generation? I wonder if a model trained to accept/ reject chains based on reference chains would do better. And even though CoT can use language, I don't see why it would need to be grammatically correct.

A measure that would be very informative is if the reasoning steps somehow arrive at the right answer, but using a faulty path. See Figure 1 here for a detailed example: https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03548
content.summary_of_the_review: I see the contribution of the new data as a strong one. Although I don't find the suite of metrics convincing, the value of the dataset still warrants acceptance. Plus, I consider the suite of metrics as an example of what can be accomplished once this data is available. I would probably give a stronger review if the data is further explored in the main text, but I am assuming the data has intrinsic value because it is human generated and am still unsure if it can be used for good downstream performance.

content.title: Response to Reviewer MQPy
content.comment:
Thank you for the comments and suggestions. Answers to your questions as well as clarifications to some of your comments below:


**The metrics mostly are intrinsic, and don't account for downstream task performance that I can tell.** As a clarification, though we do not evaluate downstream task performance explicitly by searching for answers using a template, we do include proxy metrics for this in our human annotations via the “Overall Quality” score. Additionally, there is nothing about our metrics that preclude including the final answer in the chain. Tables 12 and 40 show examples of the rationale generations used as inputs to our scorer. Many of these include answers. Though we have not yet released our full annotated datasets and code, we will do so once the anonymity period is over; it will also be easy to validate that the answer is frequently included, and frequently included as the last step, in our generations once this is released. 

**Not nearly enough analysis and exploration of the new data. For example, do these rationale lead to improved (or worse) performance? Or categorizing different types of rationale and their properties.** Thank you for this feedback. The taxonomy that we provide categorizes different types of rationales and their properties. Including rationales has already been shown in multiple papers to improve final task accuracy (see https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.11916.pdf, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.11171.pdf, among others cited in our Introduction). If the questions here are geared towards downstream implications, please see our response on “implications” to reviewer UUD9.

**It should be made more clear what are the assumptions about rationale, e.g. do we expect there to be only one valid reasoning chain?** We make no assumptions about the rationale other than constraints implied by the process used to generate them, and that process is extensively documented in our work. In particular, we do not make the assumption that there would only be one valid reasoning chain.

**I am not convinced [the metrics] would recognize an equally good but different looking rationale.** Our synthetic perturbations — on which ROSCOE correlates quite well — captures the sensitivity of our metrics to subtle differences in chains. Though we do not study the setups proposed by the reviewer explicitly in our paper, they could be interesting avenues for future investigation.  

**…the data could be more closely analyzed and I am not convinced of the usefulness of the metrics.** The intent of this work is to provide diagnostic metrics in an area for which existing metrics do not exist or are lacking and a taxonomy on an area (step-by-step rationales) for which classifications of errors currently do not exist. The authors would be very curious to hear how specifically the reviewer is defining “usefulness” in this particular part of the review; we would love to get actionable feedback for ways to strengthen our paper or as potential directions for future works. :) 

As a note, we do not expect any specific metric to be fully encompassing of all potential issues that may arise within a rationale. Rather, we assert that our suite of ROSCOE metrics are better at illustrating potential errors more strongly than prior scores on their own.    

**Faithfulness-Step: This seems very dependent on how you define steps. A chain-of-thought (CoT) can be only a few steps using multiple tokens each, and lead to deceptively high (or low) faithfulness scores. Is this the reason for the -token version?** Thank you for the observation. The challenge of having an all-encompassing single metric is the reason why we include a suite of metrics, such that downstream users can adjust for the ones most appropriate to their particular task and generation method. As mentioned in the Analysis section under “What does ROSCOE illuminate about scores across errors and tasks?”, our scores are much more sensitive than prior scores, but still require a degree of calibration for effective use. You are correct that the granularity of separation can have an impact on the sensitivity of different metrics; this is why we include multiple versions.

**Informativeness-Step: This seems counter intuitive to how CoT often works... CoT works especially well with natural language explanations, which probably will include text not in the source.** Our metrics function largely within the embedding spaces of our models; none of our metrics explicitly compare the presence or lack of specific text in the source. Commonsense error (which is an error in the general knowledge about the world, beyond what was mentioned in the source) is one type of error in our proposed Taxonomy, and was captured in evaluation perspectives (Table 15). We investigate it on Human Annotated datasets (Tables 33-39) and note that it could be challenging to catch with alignment-based methods.

content.title: Response continues
content.comment:
**Missing step: if there is a "budget" on how much can be done in the CoT, then it is potentially desirable to skip some steps and only elaborate on the most crucial ones. Also, one advantage of CoT is there are many possible reasoning chains (see self-consistency work for example).** We define “missing step” as the case where “the content of the generated reasoning is incomplete and lacks required information to produce the correct answer.” To reiterate, missing step is a step that was *required* to answer the question, but was missed by the model, which could possibly lead to a wrong answer. Furthermore, during annotation, annotators were asked “Is the reasoning in the generated response incomplete and lacking required information to produce the correct answer? Specifically, does this response contain steps that, if added in, would make for a well-supported chain?” In our correlations, we were looking if our proposed metrics can catch if any crucial information was missing from the hypothesis chain. For example, referenced-based metrics (such as “Missing step” or “Reasoning Alignment” scores) showed good correlation scores (Tables 38, 39). We refer the reviewer to our response to reviewer 8arD about “downstream tasks” for ways in which this work could be used in conjunction with self-consistency.

**Also in sec 4.4, the metrics based on perplexity seem somewhat strange. And even though CoT can use language, I don't see why it would need to be grammatically correct.** Our metrics are neural, so we can therefore create ‘perplexity-inspired’ metrics by running generation text through our models and calculating values based on inference. We explicitly make our metrics robust to scenarios where a reference score may not exist as all datasets do not include references; however, we do include reference-based metrics on datasets for which ground truth references exist - see Tables 26-31 for synthetic datasets and Tables 38 and 39 for human-annotated datasets. For the relevance of grammar, see the written response for “Faithfulness-Step”; while building our taxonomy, we noticed that there were indeed some tasks were the correctness of a rationale could be significantly impacted by grammar - for example, incorrect pronouns impact the correctness of a rational by changing anaphora resolution; tense can significantly impact the correctness of questions on temporal reasoning. 

**A measure that would be very informative is if the reasoning steps somehow arrive at the right answer, but using a faulty path.** Thank you for the feedback. An explicit measure of this would be useful and in fact this is a large motivation of our work; as mentioned in the abstract: “We simply do not know how often the stated reasoning steps actually support the final end task predictions”. Though we do not do an explicit analysis comparing when chains differ in correctness with their final answer, many of the correlations with human annotations touch on this.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a large number of metrics to evaluate step-by-step reasoning traces. They learn an embedding to evaluate similarity between steps. Authors show results on a very large and varied set of datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The authors evaluate their metrics on a large set of varied datasets with all kinds of reasoning: logical, natural and synthetic language and math.
2. This is an incredibly challenging problem and any steps towards evaluating step-by-step traces are great.


Weaknesses:
1. The authors propose a lot of metrics but have not sufficiently showed the sensitivity of each metric.
2. The method depends on having a very good similarity metrics.
3. It is not clear that the alignment metrics make sense (for example between source and hypothesis statements).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Pg1: What is the “source” in this context? 
> “and grounded with the source” 

2. The four “perspectives” could be introduced more clearly, possibly with examples and counter examples or formally with some math.

3. The authors do reference Dalvi et al. at other points in the paper, but their work should also be mentioned in the Automatic Metrics section since they have extensive step-by-step evaluation. Dalvi et al. do assume access to a ground truth trace, but their work should still be mentioned.

4. Section 3, Taxonomy: The authors should mentioned which methods, models and datasets were used to “identify nine error types”. It is important that this is representative.

5. Section 4.1: Alignment was also computed by Dalvi et al. using BLEURT and a threshold of 0.28.

6. Please make it clear at the start of 4.1 that you will use a fine-tuned embedding model. The embedding model must have a good understanding of logical reasoning for this to work in the first place? For example, how does the model deal with cases of the following flavour “The fox is red” <—> “The fox is not red” and “The dog chases the cat” <—> “The cat chases the dog”. Language models are not always good at preserving word order (tho appreciate this is a somewhat open problem).

8. I assume “cos” is the “cosine distance”?

9. It’s not clear why you could compute alignment between the source, s and the hypothesis, h? If the hypotheses has rules and facts and the source has examples of combining these, I can image that there would not be any obvious matches? Even less so for more natural language problems.

10. “Informativeness-Step (Info-Step)” appears to be a combination of other metrics and make it harder to tell is the model is (a) not using certain information or (b) hallucinating information. Combining these metrics would surely make it more difficult to tell which is occurring?

11. Why is the repetition evaluation done at the token level? If you are using a dataset like ProofWriter (or even some math datasets) it is very likely that the same token will appear in multiple steps. It would be more helpful to know of a whole step has been repeated, which is the much more common failure mode. As an example for the “valid” repeating of tokens. “1. All red things are soft, the Dax is red. Therefore the Dax is soft; 2. All soft things are cubes. The Dax is soft. Therefore, the Dax is a cube. I see there is also a “Repetition-Step metric”.

12. More general question, how do you split the outputs of the model into steps and in inputs into statements? Splitting by sentences would not accurate (example above).

13. Do I understand correctly that hallucination can only be evaluated in cases where you have a reference trace?

14. The redundancy measure makes sense. Alternatively, you could also have considered precision.

15. Self consistency metrics appear useful.

16. It is fantastic that the authors use such a wide variety of datasets!

17. For clarity, in “ROSCOE Training” what are the pairs of sentences which the authors train the model to be similar/ different to between source and hypothesis? I’m unsure how sentence in the hypothesis can be considered similar to those in the source? Especially since often sentences in the hypothesis should be some combination of those in the source?

18. For clarity, Table 3 is using the golden traces from the dataset and you are evaluating your metrics on these? Table 3 on its own must be interpreted with caution since it only shows that the metrics can identify “good” reasoning trace, but not that they can identify errors.

19. “How sensitive are ROSCOE metrics against level of errors?” rather than showing aggregated scores, it would have been more helpful to introduce the specific type of error you want to detect at the same three levels and show “error level” vs “metric”. Figure 2 goes some way to addressing this.

20. Figure 2: Why do the authors show BERT-score results on Hallucination when the other two figures do not show any Hallucination?

21. In Figure 2, I would be interested to see the repetition scores on ProofWriter.

22. Figure 2: It would be great to see a more systematic analysis applying perturbations (where possible) that related directly to each metric and showing “number/level of perturbation” vs. Metric.

23. The datasets which are used for evaluating the metric are the same datasets used to train the embedding model. How does the metric fair on out of distribution datasets?

24. Please can you give some examples of “alignments” between source and hypothesis statements for ProofWriter, EntailmentBank and GSM8k.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This is a very promising first step towards evaluating reasoning traces. My main concerns are as follows:
(1) There is insufficient systematic analysis of the proposed metrics. It would be better to propose all metrics, apply relevant perturbations and show which metrics most accurately capture the types of error they are designed for. Following this, the authors could rank the metrics in-terms of sensitivity or  suggest the top N most sensitive metrics going forward.
(2) It is not clear how the alignment process works, especially when aligning hypothesis statements with those in the source. This will also depend significantly on the model used to embed the sentences. The authors have also only shown evaluation on the same datasets that the metric was trained on.

I would be inclined to accept this paper, since it takes a very important (early) step in the right direction. It is also great that the weights for their embedding model will be available as well as their code. However, my recommendation to accept would be contingent on the authors being clear about the limitations of their approach and adding a clearly labelled section to their paper discussing these. They must also run a more systematic analysis of the perturbations and show how these affect the metrics.

content.title: Response to Reviewer mtZF
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to read our paper and write a detailed review. We have added Appendix A to the paper to discuss the limitations of our approach. 

**The authors propose a lot of metrics but have not sufficiently showed the sensitivity of each metric.** Thank you for your feedback. We report Somers’ D correlation for each error type on the Diagnostic datasets in Tables 20-25 for reference-free metrics and in Tables 26-31 for reference-based metrics. These tables also include p-values which show that the correlations are statistically significant. 

**The method depends on having a very good similarity metrics.** Thanks for your feedback, and we do agree that some of our alignment metrics depend on a similarity based model, SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021), which is a supervised sentence similarity model extending the RoBERTa word embedding model. In our experiments we ablated with finetuning SimCSE on in-domain training datasets and conducted in-depth analysis and showed in experiments results that on some domains the metrics do perform better with finetuned similarity models. This can be seen in almost all tables in the paper where we benchmark ROSCOE with baseline metrics, especially the summary tables in Appendix Tables 18, 19 and 32.  

**It is not clear that the alignment metrics make sense (for example between source and hypothesis statements).** Thanks for your comment. As we state in the paper, ROSCOE’s alignment metrics can be used reference-free and reference-based (in which case the alignment is between the hypothesis and ground-truth). However, we understand how one might think that the alignment metrics may not be informative when used between the source and hypothesis, as they are commonly used for measuring the alignment between the ground truth text and the generated hypothesis (such as machine translation or summarization tasks where ground truth usually exists). Our motivation for using reasoning alignment (for reference-free metrics) originates from the previous work that studies text-to-text information alignment to measure the information overlap between texts. For instance Egan et al. (2021), studies the decrease of the information gain from a document after observing its summary information, while Deng et al. (2021) introduced CTC (cited in the paper), which is defined as the extent to which the information in one text is grounded in another. Our reasoning alignment metrics share the same spirit and measure how much the generated rationale is grounded in the input context and the question. 

[1] Nicholas Egan, Oleg Vasilyev, and John Bohannon. 2021. Play the Shannon Game with language models: A human-free approach to summary evaluation.

[2] Mingkai Deng, Bowen Tan, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, and Zhiting Hu. Compression, transduction, and creation: A unified framework for evaluating natural language generation. In EMNLP, 2021

**The four "perspectives" could be introduced more clearly, possibly with examples and counterexamples or formally with some math.** Thanks for this feedback, we have restructured section 4 in the paper and added more examples in Tables 40-41.

**Section 3, Taxonomy: The authors should mentioned which methods, models and datasets were used to "identify nine error types".** We conducted a manual preliminary analysis on different types of LLMs reasoning errors using five Human judged datasets we used in the paper (DROP, GSM8K, ESNLI, Cosmos, SemEval). Thank you for the comment, we have updated section 3 to make this clear.  

**Please make it clear at the start of 4.1 that you will use a fine-tuned embedding model. The embedding model must have a good understanding of logical reasoning for this to work in the first place?** We compare three different sentence embedding models as mentioned in Section 6: all-mpnet-base-v2 (ROSCOE-SA1, ROSCOE-SS1), sup-simcse-roberta-base (ROSCOE-SA2, ROSCOE-SS2), and the fine-tuned SimCSE model (ROSCOE-SA, ROSCOE-SS). We found that fine-tuning on CoT helps to improve correlations, but non-finetuned sentence embedding models also work well as discussed on Pg 8, paragraph 1. As for the negation problem (“The fox is red” <—> “The fox is not red” ), we investigate it with NegateStep perturbations, and “The dog chases the cat” <—> “The cat chases the dog” is a type of Semantic Error perturbation, where we change the semantics of one step in the chain by replacing entities. Please refer to Tables 20-31 for detailed evaluations.

content.title: Response continues
content.comment:
**Why is the repetition evaluation done at the token level?** As you have noted, repetition is scored at two levels: token and sentence. Repetition-token will punish chains where there are two steps with high token overlap. In addition to the issue you mentioned, another problem with it is that it does not account for word order. Unlike Repetition-Token which is orderless, Repetition-Step considers step embeddings similarities and is more robust to changing contexts. We used both scores to understand if one performs better than another, and in most cases they behaved quite similarly (in terms of Somers’ D correlation score).

**More general question, how do you split the outputs of the model into steps and in inputs into statements? Splitting by sentences would not accurate (example above).** We separated steps with sentence ending periods. We acknowledge that this may not be perfect.

**Do I understand correctly that hallucination can only be evaluated in cases where you have a reference trace?** That depends on the dataset: hallucination showed good correlations with Info-Chain and Faithfulness-Step on most sets (Tables 20, 21, 23), but weaker on arithmetic datasets, such as MATH and AQUA (Tables 22, 25).

**For clarity, in “ROSCOE Training” what are the pairs of sentences which the authors train the model to be similar/ different to between source and hypothesis?** You are correct that sentences in the hypothesis cannot be considered similar to those in the source. That is why we fine-tuned the model by embedding source and hypothesis as a whole, not dividing them by sentences. To make it more clear, we have revised the paper to explicitly mention this in Section 5, ROSCOE Training.

**For clarity, Table 3 is using the golden traces from the dataset and you are evaluating your metrics on these?** Table 3 (Table 7 in the revised version) is based on evaluations of the perturbed golden traces. In particular, for each dataset we took all available golden traces in the test set, and added perturbations (synthetic errors) to 50% of the chains. We evaluated how well our metric can distinguish between chains with and without errors, looking at each metric and each perturbation individually (Tables 20-31). Table 3 (Table 7 in the revised version) summarizes these findings and can be interpreted as “how well different metrics can score some types of errors.”

**Figure 2: Why do the authors show BERT-score results on Hallucination when the other two figures do not show any Hallucination?** The choice of Hallucination was to pick a perturbation type for which BERTScore showed at least some separation between perturbed versus non-perturbed values within a dataset; we found that this could be quite challenging to find for baseline scores, especially baseline neural scores similar to ours. Based on this feedback, we have changed the figure for BERTScore to use Repetition, to be more in line with the other graphs. 

**In Figure 2, I would be interested to see the repetition scores on ProofWriter.** Thank you for noticing this; the scores were missing for ProofWriter by mistake. We have updated the figure appropriately.

**The datasets which are used for evaluating the metric are the same datasets used to train the embedding model. How does the metric fair on out of distribution datasets?** For Diagnostic datasets, we used the training partition of the datasets to finetune the embedding model, and performed evaluations on the test partition. We use these sets as a diagnostics to understand if we can get improvements if the model is fine-tuned on specific domains. We would like to emphasize that not all scores used the fine-tuned embedding model. In particular, in Tables 7 and 8, only ROSCOE-SA and ROSCOE-SS use the fine-tuned model, while ROSCOE-SA1,2, ROSCOE-SS1,2, ROSCOE-LI, and ROSCOE-LC use other embedding models. In addition, we evaluate our metrics on human annotated datasets to understand how well they can generalize. 

**Please can you give some examples of “alignments” between source and hypothesis statements for ProofWriter, EntailmentBank and GSM8k.** We have added more examples to Tables 40 and 41.

**Pg1: What is the “source” in this context?** We used the term ‘source’ to indicate the input context. In other words, semantic alignment metrics measure how well the generated reasoning is supported by the context. We replaced the term “source” with “source context” in this sentence for clarity.

**I assume “cos” is the “cosine distance”?** Yes, it is a cosine similarity, as introduced in Sec 4.1.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 8arD
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and feedback. Please find below the answers to your questions:

**How are human solutions performing against correct and incorrect machine-generated answers?** The reference-based metrics measure machine-generated rationales against human-written rationales. The correlations of our reference-based metrics with ground-truth error labels are reported for diagnostic datasets in Tables 19 & 26-31, and for human-judged machine-generated rationales in Tables 38 & 39. For the scope of this work, we assume human-written rationales are always correct. Please, let us know if that answers your question. We are happy to provide more information and clarifications. 

**Can you extend information about the Human Judged Datasets, including the scale and cost of work and the intent to open-source it?**  For human judged datasets annotations, we used 5 expert annotators, selected for their domain knowledge and familiarity with the relevant datasets. In general, we found that it was hard to get anonymous crowd workers to annotate our data accurately even when we paid averages of upwards of $30 an hour, which is why we elected to use expert annotators. Though these expert annotators were not paid beyond their normal salary for this work. Appendix Section F has been updated to reflect this information. We will share the data and annotations (as well as code for our paper) as soon as the anonymity period is over.

**Can you show more examples of errors in the appendix or provide access to a browser of samples (e.g., similar to https://minerva-demo.github.io/)?** We will be releasing all annotated datasets. Some examples of errors are provided in Tables 40 in Appendix H2, and we have added more examples in the revised version, including examples from Diagnostic datasets (in Appendix H2 Table 41).

**It would be interesting to see a scale of errors, that is, samples for the same problem that are correct according to the metrics, somewhat correct, somewhat incorrect, and completely incorrect.** We appreciate your feedback, but before we can provide more information, would you please clarify if the comment is asking for: 1) same exact context+question, but multiple chains, or 2) same dataset but different chains. The former of this would be challenging to construct. It would require running multiple iterations of generation and scoring to find context+hypothesis pairs that cover a wide range of scores. The latter of these would be easier, but would not be as consistent. To provide more information based on your feedback, we have extended our list of examples to highlight different cases in Table 40, and added examples from Diagnostic datasets (Table 41) in the Appendix H2. 

**The elephant in the room is the usefulness of these new evaluation metrics for downstream tasks. Does it help with re-reranking? Can we get better scores than via majority voting?** Thank you for these suggestions - these are great opportunities for future work! Due to the extensive analysis — and the amount of writing space — needed to thoroughly test and communicate the ability of these metrics to capture reasoning errors, we decided to leave some follow-up questions, such as the application of these metrics for improving downstream task performance, for future exploration. We agree that using these metrics for re-ranking would be interesting. In their recent work, Wang et. al (2022) (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.11171.pdf) has shown that sample-and-rank performs worse than majority voting so it would be interesting to see if there are good ways to tune these metrics to outperform prior ranking methods. There are also situations for which existing methods may be insufficient. For example, in cases where rationales are necessarily long, we imagine it may be important to use a scorer as a utility function to guide the partial rationale generation, similar to how a policy is used in reinforcement learning; in these scenarios, majority voting (by sampling multiple full rationale generation paths) could be used in conjunction with our scores.

**Nit: Can you explain how the frequent 1.0 score in the tables should be interpreted?** ‘1.0’ means that in the specific dataset, there is a perfect correlation between the score and the error type. In other words, we can pick a score threshold such that generated chains that have scores greater than the threshold have no errors of the given type, and generated chains that have scores less than the threshold have the given type of error present. Appendix H.1 provides an example. We have added more detailed discussion about this matter in the last part of Appendix H.1.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a new reference-free metric named ROSCOE for the step-by-step rationales that some LLMs use for reasoning tasks. The ROSCOE is a suite of metrics that cover four dimensions of step-by-step rationales (or logic chains): 1) semantic alignment, 2) semantic similarity, 3) logical inference, and 4) language coherence. The authors use five natural datasets and six diagnostic datasets for justifying the effectiveness of the proposed ROSCOE metrics. The experiments and analysis show that ROSCOE outperforms other baseline metrics such as CTC, BARTScore, and BLEURT.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

- a comprehensive and novel metric for an important problem --- to understand the quality of the step-by-step rationale (the so-called chain of thoughts). 

- very extensive experiments that compare the ROSCOE and other metrics; the reasonable choices of data and evaluation methods, and informative analysis of the behavior of ROSCOE

- a nice taxonomy of reasoning errors for analysis with perturbation in building diagnostic datasets.

## Weakness

- lack of justification for the design of many details in ROSCOE.  
- Sec 4 (especially 4.1) is hard to read. It's not a great idea to simply list all these sub-metrics without clear motivation and illustrative examples.  
- the implications of the proposed metric are relatively weak -- how to improve the rationales? what are the disadvantages of existing step-by-step rationales? these questions are not touched on. 

## Suggestions: 
- think about how future people should use this ROSCOE metric easily and for more general cases.
- can we use the ROSCOE analysis to guide the future design of the step-by-step rationale 
- what are the limitations of the proposed metrics so that people can keep that in mind when using the metrics
- what will be the methods to avoid the above limitation and fix them?

content.title: Response to Reviewer UUD9
content.comment:
Thank you so much for taking the time to read our paper and write a detailed review. Below we’ve written responses to your questions:

**Lack of justification for the design of many details in ROSCOE. Sec 4 (especially 4.1) is hard to read. It's not a great idea to simply list all these sub-metrics without clear motivation and illustrative examples.** Thank you for your feedback. While writing the paper, we found it quite challenging to balance communicating the full context of our metrics without overwhelming the reader with details so we especially appreciate the commentary on how this could be improved. Our metrics are designed as an attempt to capture errors described in the taxonomy. Based on this feedback, we have revised our presentation of metrics and changed Section 4 by improving visual presentation, as well as updating descriptions for each score with more detailed explanations. We also added more examples with evaluation scores from Human Annotated and Diagnostic sets in Tables 40 and 41. Additionally, we have added more information about how our metrics capture errors described in our taxonomy to Appendix H. We hope this will help improve the presentation and add more clarity.

**The implications of the proposed metric are relatively weak -- how to improve the rationales? what are the disadvantages of existing step-by-step rationales? these questions are not touched on.** The questions posed here are both very valid and scientifically interesting. Though our work addresses how existing step-by-step rationales lack, both by providing a taxonomy that classifies specific errors seen in datasets and offering finer-grained metrics that better correlate with specific classes of errors than previous scores, we do not tackle how to improve the rationales in this work specifically. This was due to both writing space and time limitations — our work is already quite dense as it is and it would be challenging to include these additional experiments and analysis. We do hope to tackle this in future work however. Based on the feedback here and your suggestions, we also include a Limitations section as Appendix A.
